label: late original phase (t>=5) ramping into the <DEL> step
explanation: Positional end-of-input feature. Strongest at the <DEL> delimiter step (fires on 94% of sequences there, 64% of activation mass) and also active on original-phase inputs from about the 5th/6th token onward (rate 0.67 at t=5, ~0.84 at t=6-7), activation rising step by step toward <DEL> within a sequence. Never fires at t<=2, almost never at t=3, and never in the copy phase (t>L). Top activations are at <DEL> in sequences of length 4-6 with v/i near the start (e.g. r m v v ...). Original-phase activations are weaker on repeated tokens (in_first=0 rate 0.04); most false positives are original steps at t>=5 where it stays silent, often on repeats. Token identity otherwise has little effect.

issues: The claim 'in the original phase it rarely fires on repeated tokens (rate 0.04 when in_first=0)' is false. The 0.04 rate is pooled over all phases, and copy-phase steps, which are almost all in_first=0 and never fire, drag it down. Within the original phase at t>=5, repeated tokens fire at least as often as first occurrences (test precision 0.777 for in_first==0 vs 0.758 for in_first==1). Adding in_first==1 to the predicate lowers F1 from 0.883 to 0.840 and mass recall from 0.987 to 0.919.

The false positives are not 'often on repeated tokens'. Running misses on the test split shows whole sequences where the original-phase t>=5 steps stay silent and the <DEL> step is weak or silent too (e.g. 's p f c f x m g', 'f 0 r j d o t'). The silence is a property of the whole sequence, not of a repeated current token.

Unexplained systematic modulation by the identity of the first few tokens. Precision of (phase==0)&(t>=5) depends strongly on early tokens: orig(0)=r 0.998, k 0.959, l 0.927 vs orig(0)=0 0.560, v 0.678, u 0.694; orig(2)=v 0.981, i/u 0.95 vs orig(2)=k 0.460, r 0.592, l 0.617. The explanation's line 'which token is input otherwise makes little difference' holds for the current input token but hides this strong dependence on sequence-start content. The top examples (r/k/l first, v/i at positions 1-3) show the same pattern.

Claims that check out: 0 activations in the copy phase; <DEL> active 93.6% with 63.6% of mass; original-phase rates 0.671 at t=5 and about 0.84 at t=6-7; 0 activations at t<=2 and 6 at original t=3 (the 2% active at t=3 is the <DEL> step of L=3 sequences); missed mass of 1.3%, all weak t=4 activations. Test scores reproduce exactly (P 0.827, R 0.948, F1 0.883, mass recall 0.987).

No simple better predicate found. Using t>=6 gives F1 0.813. Gating on good early tokens raises precision to 0.935 but drops F1 to 0.757. The early-token dependence is spread over many tokens, so the positional predicate stays the best simple description, but its false positives are systematic, not scattered noise.

scorecard.summary: Graded preference over the first original token (most: r, k, l, m, g, b; least: 1, q, f, c) and the previous input (most: w, k, a, l, s, z; least: 3, u, x, -); timing cues that raise it most: t=6, t=5, phase=1.
